articles.title: The catch in IBM’s offer to relocate its U.S.-based immigrant workers
articles.content:
For some IBM employees, keeping their jobs could mean moving to another country — and taking a steep pay cut in the process.

Earlier this month, IBM said it would no longer support the U.S. immigration status of workers in its consulting division, offering them the option to take a role with the company in another country or exit, according to a Bloomberg report citing a company document. 

“IBM Consulting participates in U.S. high-skilled visa programs to address skill shortages,” an IBM spokesperson told Rest of World. “That participation has been declining for a number of years, and as skill availability and client need have evolved, we have opted to discontinue visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of such roles in IBM Consulting.”

IBM Consulting employs more than 150,000 people globally. The company does not disclose the geographical split for its workforce, making it hard to ascertain the exact number of workers impacted by this decision. On November 19, the company’s career portal listed 1,278 open roles for the consulting division outside the U.S., including 1,125 in India, 23 in Singapore, and 18 in the U.K. In the U.S., it listed 89 roles.

For employees, relocation does not automatically ensure continued engagement, effective collaboration, or equal access to professional opportunities, Zakaria Laaraj, founder of consultancy Global New Ventures, told Rest of World. It may affect their access to decision-makers, established networks, and career opportunities. “The credibility of such an offer depends on employee tenure, available positions, immigration requirements, and compensation,” Laaraj said.

Discussions on Blind, an anonymous employee forum used by 14 million professionals, suggest relocating may not be realistic for many.

Moving to India, for instance, could mean an approximately 80% pay cut, one IBM employee wrote on Blind.

“Employees get three weeks to decide,” Blind’s CEO Sunguk Moon told Rest of World. “The alternative is three months of severance and a last day of December 31. And the news came in a surprise one-on-one ‘career sync’ with a manager.”

For any relocation option to be viable, companies must go beyond just assigning a new job to their employee, George Carrillo, CEO of career development and staffing company HireMe, told Rest of World.

“Moving a position can mean uprooting a family. It affects a spouse’s employment, children’s schooling, healthcare, and years of planning. HR should provide clear options, deadlines, and coordinated support. Leaders must own the follow-through,” Carrillo said.

Most U.S. tech giants are navigating the challenges arising from changing visa norms under Donald Trump’s leadership.

“IBM has an advantage because it already operates international offices with the infrastructure and staff to absorb those workers,” Lacey Kaelani, CEO of job search engine Metaintro, told Rest of World. “Rather than abandoning the talent, companies like IBM can move the work to where the talent is.” 

Earlier this year, Amazon allowed stranded H-1B workers to work from India amid consular delays but only temporarily. Microsoft defended its international talent hiring strategy in an October blog post pushing back against the U.S. administration’s allegations that it replaces American workers with foreign visa holders. The statement followed its suspension from the Department of Labor’s PERM green card program alongside Adobe and six other IT outsourcing firms, including TCS and Infosys. 

“Companies are looking for solutions, but they’re also making business decisions,” Cassandra Fultz, co-founder of Doherty Fultz Immigration, told Rest of World. “Sponsoring an employee indefinitely, particularly when the outcome is uncertain, can be expensive and disruptive. Moving that employee to an existing operation abroad may be an option with more stability for the business. That doesn’t mean every employee will be offered the opportunity for placement abroad. Each country has its own eligibility requirements and work authorization rules. Companies will inevitably prioritize the people and positions they consider most valuable or difficult to replace.”

Even employees are reevaluating the lure of the American Dream as the uncertainty tax of constant visa changes weighs heavily on them. The wait for green cards for Indian nationals — who typically receive three-quarters of the H-1B visas and comprise the majority of the green card queue — can take several decades, according to the National Foundation for American Policy. Even with Democrats winning control of both the House and the Senate, immigration issues will stay with the White House and executive agencies. 

“Mid-career professionals in the queue for green cards are most impacted,” Abhijit Bhaduri, former general manager for global learning and development at Microsoft and author of the upcoming book AIdentity: How to Become Irreplaceable in the New World of Work, told Rest of World. “They built a life in a country that still lists them as temporary. A visa is a document. But the vanishing green card queue feels like a broken promise. They followed every rule for years, and the finish line moved. You can relocate a job overnight. Rebuilding and redesigning a new identity takes years. That is the invisible price that gets missed.”

articles.title: Florida Law Allowing Bar Liability for Knowingly Serving "Habitually Addicted" Doesn't Apply When Server Only Saw One Drinking Session
articles.content:
From Croteau v. Family 5, Inc., decided Wednesday by Florida Court of Appeal Chief Judge Jonathan Gerber, joined by Judges Marlon Weiss and Johnathan Lott:

In this personal injury case, the plaintiff appeals from the circuit court's final summary judgment which found … that the plaintiff could not prove her negligence action against a bar which had served her alcoholic beverages before she was injured later that night. The summary judgment rested on the circuit court's application of "the dram shop statute"—section 768.125, Florida Statutes (2020):

Liability for injury or damage resulting from intoxication. A person who sells or furnishes alcoholic beverages to a person of lawful drinking age shall not thereby become liable for injury or damage caused by or resulting from the intoxication of such person, except that a person who willfully and unlawfully sells or furnishes alcoholic beverages to a person who is not of lawful drinking age or who knowingly serves a person habitually addicted to the use of any or all alcoholic beverages may become liable for injury or damage caused by or resulting from the intoxication of such minor or person.

The underlined second exception is at issue here…. In addressing "what constitutes 'knowledge' in order for a vendor's conduct to be found negligent," the [Florida Supreme Court has] found:

[T]he cause of action [under section 768.125's second exception] only requires evidence that the vendor had knowledge that the individual the vendor served was a habitual drunkard. Serving an individual multiple drinks on one occasion would be insufficient, in and of itself, to establish that the vendor knowingly served a habitual drunkard alcoholic beverages. On the other hand, serving an individual a substantial number of drinks on multiple occasions would be circumstantial evidence to be considered by the jury in determining whether the vendor knew that the person was a habitual drunkard….

[In another case,] we affirmed a summary judgment for the defendant bar, where the plaintiff patron was unknown to the bar's staff, was not a bar regular, and had purchased up to four drinks over two to three hours. We held that we could not impute notice of the patron's alcohol addiction to the bar when the patron had not shown any signs of intoxication, despite his alcohol consumption ….

Here, consistent with [those precedents], the bar's serving the alcoholic beverages to the plaintiff for the first time on the incident date, without more, should not be considered sufficient evidence to impute knowledge to the bar that the plaintiff was "habitually addicted to the use of any or all alcoholic beverages." …

Roster v. Moulton (Fla. App. 1992)—the primary case upon which the plaintiff relies—is distinguishable….

[In Roster,] [i]t is undisputed that [the patron] consumed 8–10, 12–ounce cans of beer and two straight shots of tequila over the period of an hour and a half. After a short absence from [the bar], during which [the patron] drank yet another beer served elsewhere, [the patron] returned to [the bar's] walk-up window, where he ordered and was served another beer. The [bar manager] admitted that it would be unusual for a person to consume that many beers and two shots of tequila without showing signs of intoxication. Despite [the patron's] considerable alcohol consumption, [the patron] did not stagger and did not slur his speech. The manager twice asked [the patron] to leave the bar only because [the patron] became loud and argumentative. [The patron] pled guilty to the charge of driving while under the influence of alcohol and admitted that he had a drinking problem from the age of sixteen, which he still had at the time of the accident. At that time, [the patron] had never received treatment for his alcohol addiction….

By affidavit in Roster, "two experts[] … essentially stated that the large amount of alcohol that [the patron had] consumed over a relatively short time period, together with the lack of impairment [which the patron had] demonstrated, would have put a reasonable server of alcohol on notice that [the patron] was habitually addicted to alcohol. [The bar] submitted no affidavits to oppose these viewpoints." …

However, unlike in Roster, as the bar's answer brief submits:

… [W]hatever alcohol [the plaintiff] may have consumed at [the bar], she claims she drank over a five-hour period—much longer than the 90 minutes during which the Roster [patron] consumed 10–12 drinks. Furthermore, [the plaintiff] claims she sat, ordered drink(s), and watched television for five hours, which is much different than the Roster [patron,] who left the bar …, drank another alcoholic beverage elsewhere, and then came back to the bar where he was served yet another drink. Also, unlike … in Roster, there is no evidence that [the plaintiff] demonstrated a level of intoxication consistent with someone who had either a high or low tolerance for alcohol. Finally, unlike the [patron] in Roster, [the plaintiff here] did not become loud or argumentative at the [bar]. By her own admission, she was quiet, not boisterous, not loud, not abusive, and she simply kept to herself….

Unlike the Roster patron, the plaintiff here was an anonymous patron, whose behavior during her visit to the bar was, by her own statements, unremarkable.

Judge Lott agreed, but added that he thought Roster was wrongly decided, including in its reliance on expert evidence:

Section 768.125, Florida Statutes (2020), says that a bar owner is not liable for damage caused by the sale of alcoholic beverages, except that (as relevant here) a person "who knowingly serves a person habitually addicted to the use of any or all alcoholic beverages may become liable." The language does not require expert testimony, and does not ask how the latest version of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) defines pathologies related to alcohol use….

The statutory language asks whether the server has actual knowledge that the person is, as a matter of habit, addicted to alcohol…. You know such a thing when you see it—and it's hard to imagine being able to see it given only a single occasion of indulgence…. [A]nyone can have too many drinks. What separates a "habitual drunkard" [which is how the concurrence elsewhere interprets "habitually addicted"] is that the habitual drunkard feels compelled to do so on account of their addiction, and does so regularly as a matter of habit….

Turning back to Roster—where was the evidence that the defendant actually knew that the plaintiff was habitually addicted to alcohol? The defendant observed the plaintiff drink heavily on one occasion wherein he handled his liquor well, until he didn't. No evidence of "addiction" was presented, much less of a "habit" of it. The expert affidavits about his apparent alcohol tolerance added nothing to that inquiry.

In sum, Roster passed the buck from the statutory language to expert opinion, and reached the wrong result in turn. In an appropriate case, we should consider whether to recede from it….

Jack R. Reiter and Robert C. Weill (GrayRobinson, P.A.) represent the bar.

articles.title: Former Dragon Age boss questions whether BioWare should have become 'a one project studio' dropping either Mass Effect or Dragon Age to survive EA
articles.author: Elie Gould
articles.content:
"I think the version of BioWare that survives EA better is a version where we drop down to one franchise at a time, maybe just one franchise at all. Maybe we just carve SWTOR off and they become an independent studio within EA, because I don't know how what I'm about to say makes sense if you don't do that. But you ship Mass Effect, you ship Dragon Age, and then one of those wins—I hate this—one of those wins and then you just become a one-project studio. There are lots of studios within EA that did that and it didn't work—they still got murdered in their sleep, so maybe that doesn't work anyway." Via an interview with Pembridge.

Many are asking themselves how a legendary studio like BioWare, which is responsible for staples of the PC gaming genre like Neverwinter Nights, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, and the OG Baldur's Gate, alongside Mass Effect and Dragon Age, can be shuttered.

Former Dragon Age executive producer Mark Darrah has already explained how the studio was backed into a corner by EA. Escalating financial pressure led to the poor decisions and subpar games we saw ahead of BioWare's closure. But what if it had all gone differently? Despite everything, Darrah does question whether there was a way for BioWare to survive under EA.

"BioWare's entire existence under EA—it was essentially zero sum, if somebody was getting resources it was coming at the expense of somebody else," Darrah explains. "It's almost like BioWare has run exactly the same way for its entire existence. But the external constraints were different. So in the early days when BioWare needed more people it hired more people. That's like Baldur's Gate 1, Neverwinter Nights, in the early days when we have all these different threads and branches.

"And then in 2007/2008, when the EA constraints come in, the same desires are there, we need more people to ship our games so the way we fix that in that time period is by cutting off all those other branches. So [Jade Empire sequel] Revolver goes away and the Handheld [Development] Group goes away … and so Dragon Age and Mass Effect eats everything."

The alternative? Scaling things down to meet EA's needs. "Budgets keep going up, but we're still not getting bigger… So what's happening is that the walls are closing in and we're trying to be three things [SWTOR, Mass Effect, Dragon Age] and arguably we can only afford to be two things, or one thing." There's no telling whether this would've saved BioWare, but it has worked for other studios.

"Maxis figured out how to live inside of EA and BioWare never did," Darrah adds. Focusing on just one project does seem to be the answer, or at least Darrah believes it has been for Maxis and Battlefield Studios, which both had games that initially underperformed and weren't well received. "If [Battlefield Studios] don't work on Battlefield then you might as well shut the studio down. So they all work on Battlefield 4 and they fix Battlefield 4 and it becomes successful, like very successful after the fact. The Sims 4, same thing."

On the other hand "Mass Effect Andromeda ships and then Dragon Age 4 which has been starving for resources is like 'No, no [the devs] are supposed to come to us. Where are they?' That need to keep them in place isn't there in the same way. So when I say BioWare didn't adapt to EA, that's what I mean."

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

Elie is a news writer with an unhealthy love of horror games—even though their greatest fear is being chased. When they're not screaming or hiding, there's a good chance you'll find them testing their metal in metroidvanias or just admiring their Pokemon TCG collection. Elie has previously worked at TechRadar Gaming as a staff writer and studied at JOMEC in International Journalism and Documentaries – spending their free time filming short docs about Smash Bros. or any indie game that crossed their path.

articles.title: Oscar Wilde had a surprising rapport with Colorado miners – why it is hard to imagine that happening today
articles.author: Joshua Fagan
articles.content:
Oscar Wilde, the Victorian writer of “The Picture of Dorian Gray” and “The Importance of Being Earnest,” was a fashionable icon known as much for his refined manner and conversation as for his writings.

So the image of Wilde exploring Colorado’s frontier towns and rugged mines sounds like a scene from a dream. But that is exactly what happened during his extensive tour of the U.S. in 1882.

Wilde arrived in the U.S. from Europe with much aplomb. The impresario Richard D’Oyly Carte, the promoter of the acclaimed operetta duo W.S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan, bankrolled Wilde’s tour.

Gilbert and Sullivan had recently written a new comic opera, “Patience,” which mocked the aesthetic movement, of which Wilde was an icon. Championing artifice and refinement in all aspects of life, aesthetes dressed in ornate, unusual ways, such as Wilde’s habit of wearing an unnatural green carnation on his lapel. The often-mocked figure of the dandy, a wealthy man who dressed in the most bizarre and fanciful fashions of day, was an inspiration for aesthetes.

I study 19th-century literature in the English-speaking world, and I see Wilde’s western journey to my home state of Colorado as an example of how intellectual writers in the Victorian era were interested in the working class and how that curiosity was, perhaps surprisingly, mutual.

Wilde’s journey to the ‘Wild West’

Carte brought Wilde to America around the time of the U.S. premiere of “Patience” to help popularize the idea of the aesthete. While on tour, Wilde visited major cities, such as New York and Philadelphia, giving almost 100 interviews. But he also was interested in the “Wild West.” His curiosity may seem paradoxical: Tawdry saloons and dusty main streets were a stark contrast to the atmosphere of luxurious refinement he cultivated.

Yet, above all, Wilde craved the novel and unexpected. He sought experiences and people who were the opposite of the conventionality he saw as chaining Victorian society. The slightly anarchic roughness of the West appealed to him. He called it “the most beautiful part” of the country.

Wilde arrived in Colorado Springs in April 1882. Railroad baron William Jackson Palmer had founded this booming resort town in 1871. The town, a short railway journey from Denver, served as a health retreat for those suffering from tuberculosis – one of the deadliest diseases in the nation at the time.

Befitting its growing popularity, Colorado Springs had a thriving arts scene. According to the Colorado Springs Pioneers Museum, “interest in the arts began almost immediately” and was distinguished by the opening of an opera house in 1881. Crafting it in red brick and sandstone, the architects took inspiration from Madison Square Theater in New York. It became one of the most impressive buildings in the state.

Wilde gave his lecture on “The Decorative Arts” at this opera house. He did not condescend to his Colorado audience, nor did he suggest that the highest quality art could only exist in the refined settings of Europe. Instead, he insisted that art should be a part of ordinary existence.

“Art,” he declared, “is not something which you can take or leave” but rather “a necessity of human life.” For Wilde, art meant “value to the workman” and “the pleasure which he must necessarily take in making a beautiful thing.” The quality of art for Wilde was not about luxury and extravagance but about creativity and honesty in creation.

The local paper, The Daily Gazette – now The Gazette – reviewed his talk positively in a column from April 15, 1882. The column praises Wilde for how “the entire evening he commanded the closest attention of his audience.” Reportedly, when he “would give expression to a brilliant thought or idea a murmur of applause would pass through the audience.” The article finishes by exclaiming that the lecture “was instructive and interesting and appreciated by all who were present.”

A dandy among the miners

Wilde’s popularity in the West reveals the oversimplistic nature of the divide between the “highbrow” culture of the literati and the culture of “common” society.

His visit to the isolated, high-elevation mountain town of Leadville makes this blending of “high” and “low” culture even more vital. In this hardscrabble town, which owed its existence to the hard labor of miners, workers came to the Tabor Opera House to hear the lavish aesthete. Similar to his speech in Colorado Springs, he discussed how “beautiful and rational designs are necessary in all work.”

For Wilde, the roughness of his surroundings were closer to his ideal than the conventionality of Eastern U.S. cities, with their “bad wall-papers horribly designed.”

The relationship between Wilde and his Leadville audience was symbiotic. The artist found what he desired in the hard-edged mountain town, far from the pomp and conventions of Europe.

“The revolver was their book of etiquette,” Wilde wrote of the town, not altogether disapprovingly.

He drank with miners, some of whom lowered him into the depths of the Matchless Mine, a riotous atmosphere he found rather exciting.

The miners, he wrote in his “Impressions of America,” were “very charming and not at all rough.” According to Wilde, these miners likewise found value in his discussions about art.

Beyond the ‘highbrow-lowbrow’ divide

Newspaper articles about Wilde’s lectures in Colorado do not emphasize the cultural gap between him and his audiences. That dynamic may not have seemed odd – other than the novelty of a foreign celebrity visiting towns in the interior of the country.

In addition, 19th-century literary culture may not have conceived of the rigid divide between highbrow literati interests and those of the working class that exists today. The historian Lawrence Levine, in his influential 1990 book “Highbrow/Lowbrow,” asserts that supposedly elite pursuits actually had wide appeal in 19th-century American culture.

For instance, opera was not associated primarily with multimillionaires in fancy tuxedos and evening gowns, but was also a popular pastime for all ages and social classes. That opera houses even existed in the frontier towns of Colorado demonstrates Levine’s point.

Working-class residents of Leadville appreciated the chance to hear Wilde lecture about art as much as he relished the chance to travel to a real mining town and talk with its residents.

In my view, economic and cultural divides of today can be bridged so everyone can engage intellectual insights and reflections. Witty, sophisticated authors like Wilde do not simply belong to exclusive elite circles.
